basis: Review date: 2026-09-30. Codex reviewed retained question and warmup captures across all 26 lesson and checkpoint flows; sampled first-run, Learn, Progress, Settings and linked problem frames; and checked the relevant Swift and crawl JSON. This is a source and retained-capture audit against baseline e38914d with uncommitted audit tooling. It is not a new native crawl. The original 1,246 screenshots were retained, though not every frame was independently inspected. Physical VoiceOver, backup roundtrip, notification delivery, and the full English, dark-mode and AX5 matrix were outside this pass. No app fix is claimed here.
flag_note: The original crawler labels, small-target checks, unlabeled-control checks and no-change checks are automated observations. Exact 44-point comparisons can flag values such as 43.999984741; nested controls can share the same bounds and make a blank child look like a separate unlabeled button. Confirm the actual hit area and spoken output before treating these as app defects.

claude_assessments.text: Confirmed in the captured 2-player crash and the current PlayView indexing path. Opening the policy detail for a table with fewer than four seats can read past styles. This is the most urgent fix because it terminates a normal play flow.

Confirmed in the retained answer/reveal pairs and RangeRead grading and explanation code. The success band and sentence use different criteria; learners can receive a correct mark with a narrowing warning, or a wrong mark with a reassuring explanation.

Confirmed for the captured first viewport. The hand is obscured when the decision sheet first opens, then becomes visible after scrolling. The problem is the extra scroll before deciding, not permanent loss of the cards.
Confirmed for the captured first viewport of the free table. The raise control is reachable after scrolling; its initial placement under the tab bar creates the extra step and weakens its visibility.

Confirmed by comparing the captured locked and unlocked states. ConceptDrillView.swift:931-939 disables answers until the final action, while the shared GTChoiceButton styling in Components.swift:846-865 does not visibly distinguish the disabled state. The small instruction line carries the entire state change.
Visible in the cited scrolled captures: content can pass beneath the top controls and obscure a heading. The retained frames establish this on those routes, not on every table screen or device size.

The captured nested example has no dedicated close control, and returning through back or swipe takes more effort. ConceptDrillView.swift:847-852 shows that the outer explanation sheet does have a close button, so this applies only to the nested example. It is a navigation clarity issue whose impact needs a learner test.

The captured confirmation and destination support the route mismatch. PlayView.swift:143-146 leaves the finished table; ProgressionModel.swift:814-817 clears it; and PlayView.swift:80-103 returns to Play home rather than setup. The wording should make this destination clear or route directly to setup.
The term appears in the captured hand review without an adjacent explanation. This is a plausible beginner comprehension issue; no learner test was run to measure the effect.

The empty card follows from the demo fixture: ProgressionModel seeds historical aggregates but no dailySummaries, and RecordsView derives this card from dailySummaries. It is not a confirmed defect in real progress. A real persisted-progress case was not tested.

codex_findings.title: Graded Position questions display the answer order before commitment
codex_findings.detail: The seat diagram in a graded Position question shows the learner's highlighted seat beside the actual preflop or postflop action order. ConceptDrillView.swift:1058-1079 builds that order before the learner answers, while Position.swift:29 derives the correct choice from the same order. In the captured CO question, counting seats to the right gives the answer, 3. The diagram is useful in guided practice, but the graded question can be solved from the displayed answer order rather than recalling position. Keep the scaffold in guided help, or explicitly present the graded drill as supported practice. This is a learning-design inference from source and captures, not a measured effect on mastery.
codex_findings.card_note: The graded question shows the same action order used to derive its answer before commitment.

codex_findings.title: Range evidence is too small to compare individual hands
codex_findings.detail: In the Range Read reveal and EV loss range, the 13×13 grid compresses hand labels to about 6 pt on the captured default-size phone. RangeGridView.swift:75-77 fixes the label at max(6, side × 0.30); ConceptDrillView.swift:1722 constrains the Range Read grid to 250 pt, and the EV screen to roughly 230 pt high. The colored overview remains useful, but reading which hands were missed or added requires very close inspection. Add an expandable chart or a readable text summary of missed and extra hands while keeping the overview. RangeGridView.swift:123-131 provides accessibility labels for rows while cells are hidden from accessibility; this finding is about visual legibility, and VoiceOver behavior was not tested here.
codex_findings.card_note: The fixed ~6 pt grid labels make individual hand comparison difficult; offer a readable enlargement or missed/extra hand list.

codex_findings.title: Calling ranges are mislabeled as top-strength ranges
codex_findings.detail: Archetype.swift:62-67 builds a calling range by removing raising hands from the playable range. It therefore is not simply the strongest N% of hands, yet RangeRead.swift:130,141-142 describes it as ‘상위 N%’ and ‘top N%’. RangeGridView.swift:123-131 repeats the generic top-percent wording in its accessibility summary. That wording can teach the wrong shape for a call range even when the learner's width is close. Describe it as ‘전체 조합의 N%’ / ‘N% of combinations’ and explain that raising hands have been removed.
codex_findings.card_note: Calling hands exclude raising hands; ‘상위 N%’ implies a top-strength slice that the chart does not represent.
